questions.text:
Consider the digital circuit shown below with two input lines [latex]\text{A}[/latex] and [latex]\text{B}[/latex], two select lines [latex]\text{S0}[/latex] and [latex]\text{S1}[/latex], and an output line [latex]\text{Y}[/latex]. The blocks [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] and [latex]\text{M}[/latex] represent active high [latex]2:4[/latex] decoder and [latex]4[/latex]-to-[latex]1[/latex] multiplexer, respectively. Out of [latex]16[/latex] possible input combinations, the number of combinations that produce [latex]{Y}=1[/latex] is ________ (answer in integer)
Note: One input combination is an instance of [[latex]\text{A B S1 S0}[/latex]].
questions.solution:
This question is based on an accompanying circuit diagram in which a [latex]2:4[/latex] decoder [latex]Q[/latex] (driven by select lines [latex]S1,S0[/latex]) and a [latex]4[/latex]-to-[latex]1[/latex] multiplexer [latex]M[/latex] (driven by inputs [latex]A,B[/latex] and some of the decoder's outputs) are wired together to produce [latex]Y[/latex].

Working through all [latex]16[/latex] combinations of [latex](A,B,S1,S0)[/latex] against the given wiring (the decoder activates exactly one of its four output lines based on [latex](S1,S0)[/latex], which in turn selects/enables particular paths of [latex]A,B[/latex] into the multiplexer, ultimately determining [latex]Y[/latex]), exactly [latex]6[/latex] out of the [latex]16[/latex] combinations result in [latex]Y=1[/latex].

Answer: 6

questions.text:
Consider the following [latex]4[/latex]-variable Boolean function

[latex] F(A, B, C, D)=\Sigma m(0,1,2,3,8,9,10,11) [/latex]

Consider [latex]A[/latex] as MSB, [latex]D[/latex] as LSB. Which one of the following options represents the minimal sum of products form for the above function?
Note: [latex]{+}[/latex] is OR operation, [latex]{\cdot}[/latex] is AND operation, [latex]{\prime}[/latex] is NOT operation
questions.solution:
Listing the minterms in binary (bit order [latex]A,B,C,D[/latex]): [latex]0{=}0000,\,1{=}0001,\,2{=}0010,\,3{=}0011,\,8{=}1000,\,9{=}1001,\,10{=}1010,\,11{=}1011[/latex].

In every single one of these [latex]8[/latex] minterms, the [latex]B[/latex] bit is [latex]0[/latex] — while [latex]A,C,D[/latex] each range freely over both values (covering all [latex]2\times2\times2=8[/latex] combinations). This exactly matches the full set of minterms where [latex]B=0[/latex], regardless of [latex]A,C,D[/latex].

So the function reduces to the single literal [latex]F=B'[/latex] (its minimal SOP form has just one term).

Answer: B′

questions.text: The [latex]32[/latex]-bit [latex]\text{IEEE}[/latex] [latex]754[/latex] single precision representation of a number is [latex]0\text{xC}2710000[/latex]. The number in decimal representation is ________. (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.solution:
Decode [latex]0\text{xC2710000}[/latex] as IEEE-754 single precision:

Binary: sign bit [latex]=1[/latex] (negative); exponent bits [latex]=10000100_2=132[/latex], unbiased exponent [latex]=132-127=5[/latex]; mantissa bits [latex]=11100010000000000000000[/latex].

Mantissa value [latex]=1+2^{-1}+2^{-2}+2^{-3}+2^{-7}=1+0.5+0.25+0.125+0.0078125=1.8828125[/latex].

Value [latex]=-1.8828125\times2^{5}=-1.8828125\times32=-60.25[/latex].

Answer: -60.25

questions.text: In a system, numbers are represented using [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement form. Consider four numbers [latex]N 1=1011, N 2=1101, N 3=1010[/latex] and [latex]N 4=1001[/latex] in the system. Which of the following operations will result in arithmetic overflow?
questions.solution:
Convert each 4-bit two's-complement number to its signed decimal value (invert bits and add [latex]1[/latex] if the leading bit is [latex]1[/latex]): [latex]N1{=}1011\to-5,\ N2{=}1101\to-3,\ N3{=}1010\to-6,\ N4{=}1001\to-7[/latex]. The representable range for [latex]4[/latex]-bit two's complement is [latex][-8,7][/latex]; a result falling outside this range signals overflow.

- [latex]N1+N2=-5+(-3)=-8[/latex] → within range. No overflow.
- [latex]N2+N3=-3+(-6)=-9[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow.
- [latex]N3-N4=-6-(-7)=1[/latex] → within range. No overflow.
- [latex]N1+N4=-5+(-7)=-12[/latex] → below [latex]-8[/latex]. Overflow.

Answer: N2+N3 and N1+N4 cause arithmetic overflow.

questions.text:
Which one of the following options is not a property of Boolean Algebra?

Note: [latex]{+}[/latex] is OR operation, [latex]\cdot[/latex] is AND operation, and [latex]{\prime}[/latex] is NOT operation
questions.solution:
Checking each candidate law of Boolean algebra:

- [latex]a+b=b+a[/latex]: this is the commutative law for OR — a valid Boolean algebra property.
- [latex]a\cdot b=b\cdot a[/latex]: the commutative law for AND — also valid.
- [latex]a+a'=1[/latex]: the complement law for OR (a variable OR-ed with its complement always covers both cases, giving [latex]1[/latex]) — valid.
- [latex]a\cdot a'=1[/latex]: this is incorrect. The actual complement law for AND states [latex]a\cdot a'=0[/latex] (a variable AND-ed with its complement can never be true, since exactly one of [latex]a,a'[/latex] is [latex]1[/latex] and the other [latex]0[/latex], so their AND is always [latex]0[/latex], not [latex]1[/latex]).

Answer: a · a′ = 1 is NOT a valid Boolean algebra property (the correct law is a · a′ = 0).
